problem: The trap states the opposite of the truth: it says the 0.2% offset does not start at 0.2 on a percentage axis. On a percentage-strain axis, 0.2% strain is exactly the number 0.2, so the offset line must be started at 0.2 there, and at 0.002 only on a strain axis. As written, a student is taught to start at the wrong point on a percentage axis.
fix: The 0.2% offset starts at strain 0.002. If the axis is percentage strain, start at 0.2 on that axis; if the axis is plain strain, start at 0.002. Check which axis the question uses.

problem: The mild-steel curve runs from [18, 400] straight down to [24, 0], so the plotted breaking stress is 0 MPa. The text says the breaking stress is only slightly lower than the UTS, and no material fractures at zero engineering stress. A student reading the figure will conclude that the breaking stress is zero.
fix: End the MS curve at a non-zero breaking stress, for example [20, 400], [24, 350], then show the drop to zero as a separate vertical fall at fracture, with a note that the breaking stress is the last non-zero value computed with A₀.

problem: The initial straight part goes from [0, 0] to [0.2%, 229 MPa]. Its slope is 229/0.002 = 114 500 MPa ≈ 115 GPa, about half the 200 GPa that steel actually has, and the text tells the student that this slope is Young's modulus. Anyone reading E off the figure gets a wrong number.
fix: Put the proportional limit and yield at about 0.11% strain, e.g. [0.11, 229], so the slope is 229/0.0011 ≈ 208 000 MPa ≈ 200 GPa, and extend the plateau from there; or state in the caption that the elastic part is drawn exaggerated so E cannot be read from the figure.

problem: The text says brittle cast iron shows under 1% elongation, but the CI curve breaks at 1.2% strain. The two statements disagree.
fix: Move the CI fracture point to about 0.8% strain, e.g. [0.4, 220], [0.8, 250], then the fall, keeping the text at under 1%.

problem: The lower yield point is the minimum stress at the bottom of the drop, not the flat part. The flat part is the yield plateau (Lüders band spreading along the gauge length).
fix: The peak is the upper yield point, the dip that follows is the lower yield point, and the flat stretch after it is the yield plateau.
